title: The rich man's rules
translation: A very rich man once said:
"Put everything else aside and get rich. If you're poor, life isn't worth living. Only the rich count as people.

If you want to get rich, the first thing to train is your attitude. And the attitude is this: live as if the world will go on for ever, and never, not even for a moment, think about how nothing lasts. That's rule one.

Rule two: don't satisfy every need. As long as you live, you'll want endless things, for yourself and for others. Follow your desires and try to get them all, and even a million coins won't stay with you for a moment. Wants never stop. Money runs out. You can't feed endless wants with limited money. When a want starts to stir in you, take it as an evil thought that has come to ruin you. Be on your guard, be afraid of it, and don't spend anything, not even on small things.
Rule three: if you think money is a servant you can use as you like, you'll never get out of poverty. Respect it and fear it like your lord, like a god. Never order it around.
Rule four: even if someone humiliates you, don't get angry and don't hold a grudge.
Rule five: be honest and keep your promises.

Live by these rules while you go after profit, and wealth will come to you the way fire goes to dry wood and water runs downhill. Once the money piles up and never runs out, you don't spend it on parties, drink, music or women. You don't decorate your house. You don't get what you want. But your mind is always at peace, and you're happy."

But people want money so they can get what they want. Money is worth something because it gets you things. If you want things and don't get them, and you have money and don't use it, you're no different from a poor man. Where's the pleasure in that?

As far as I can see, his rules just mean this: give up wanting things, and you won't mind being poor. Better to have no money at all than to make satisfying your wants your pleasure. Someone with a nasty boil enjoys washing it in water, but it's better not to have the boil.
Taken this far, rich and poor are the same thing. The last stage of enlightenment is the same as the first. Great greed looks a lot like no greed at all.

literal: A certain very rich man said: 'A person should put aside all things and single-mindedly acquire wealth.
If poor, there is no point in living.
Only the rich are counted as people.
If you want to acquire wealth, you must first of all train that attitude.
That attitude is nothing else.
Dwell in the thought that the human world is permanent, and do not even for a moment contemplate impermanence.
This is the first precaution.
Next, do not satisfy the needs of all things.
While a person is in the world, for oneself and for others, wishes are without measure.
If you think to follow desire and achieve your aims, even if you have a million coins, they will not stay even for a moment.
Wishes have no time of stopping.
Wealth has a time of running out.
To serve limitless wishes with limited wealth is impossible.
If a wish stirs in your heart, (think) that an evil thought has come that would destroy you, be firmly cautious and afraid, and do not do even a small expense.
Next, if you regard money as something to use like a servant, you will not escape poverty for long.
Fear and revere it like a lord, like a god, and do not use it as if it obeyed you.
Next, even if you meet with shame, do not be angry or resentful.
Next, be honest and keep promises firmly.
For a person who keeps these principles and seeks profit, the coming of wealth will be like fire going to what is dry and water following what is low.

When money accumulates and does not run out, (you) do not make a business of banquets, drink, music and women, do not decorate your dwelling, and though you do not fulfil your wishes, your mind is for ever at ease and happy', he said.
After all, people seek wealth in order to fulfil their wishes.
That money is counted as wealth is because it grants wishes.
To have wishes but not fulfil them, to have money but not use it, is entirely the same as a poor person.
What would one take as pleasure?
This rule sounds as if it is simply: cut off human desires and do not grieve over poverty.
Rather than making desire one's pleasure, nothing is better than having no wealth.
Rather than a person suffering from a boil taking pleasure in washing it with water, nothing is better than not having the illness.
When it comes to this, there is no distinction between poor and rich.
The highest stage is equal to the lowest stage.
Great desire resembles no desire.

notes.text: {長者|ちやうじや}: 'a rich man' (modern {億万長者|おくまんちやうじや}, 'billionaire'). {大福|だいふく}: 'great fortune'. Kenkō does not name him.

notes.quote: 一向に徳をつくべきなり
notes.text: {徳|とく} here is 'wealth, gain' (as in {得|とく}), not 'virtue'. The 1925 edition: to get riches for oneself. {一向|ひたぶる}に: 'single-mindedly' (the edition's reading).

notes.quote: 人間常住の思ひに住して
notes.text: {常住|じやうぢゆう}: 'permanent, never changing', the Buddhist opposite of {無常|むじやう}, impermanence. The rich man's first rule turns upside down the teaching that runs through the whole book (see sections 7 and 137).

notes.quote: 万事の用をかなふべからず
notes.text: {用|よう}: 'a need, something that has to be paid for'. かなふ: 'to grant, to satisfy'.
{銭|ぜに}: copper coins, most of them imported from China at the time. A million was a fortune.
{小用|せうよう}: 'a small expense, a little errand' (the 1925 edition's gloss).
{奴|やつこ}: a servant (see section 211). The rule reverses the usual order: money is the master, you serve it.

notes.quote: 火の乾けるに就き、水の下れるに従ふ
notes.text: From the Chinese Book of Changes, as the 1925 edition notes: 'water flows to what is wet, fire goes to what is dry' (水流濕、火就燥). A picture of something that happens by itself, with no effort.
Feasts, drinking, music and sex (the 1925 edition: banquets, music and lust).
そもそも: 'but in the first place'. Kenkō's answer starts here.
{癰疽|ようそ}: dangerous swellings and boils with high fever (the 1925 edition's gloss). Desire is the boil; spending money on it is the water.

Tendai Buddhism counts six stages from an ordinary person to a Buddha. {理即|りそく} is the lowest: you have the Buddha-nature in you but have not woken up to it. {究竟|くきやう} is the highest, full enlightenment (both from the 1925 edition's glosses). The highest stage being equal to the lowest is a Buddhist paradox: everyone already has the Buddha-nature.
Still a Japanese proverb today. Here it sums up the section: the rich man wants so much that, in practice, he lives as if he wanted nothing.
